stem:
A patient has a suspected ectopic pregnancy. She is hemodynamically stable, has no severe pain, and an adnexal mass is seen.

Which factor most strongly favors medical management with methotrexate rather than immediate surgery?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Signs of rupture (acute abdomen, haemodynamic instability) are an absolute contraindication to methotrexate and mandate urgent surgical intervention.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Methotrexate works over days, so it needs β-hCG on day 4 and day 7 and a prompt return for new pain. RANZCOG reserves it for women who are clinically stable and can reliably come back for review.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Inability to follow up is a contraindication to MTX, not an indication — without serial β-hCG, treatment failure or rupture cannot be detected in time.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Suggests intraperitoneal bleeding or rupture — surgical emergency. MTX requires the absence of acute peritoneal irritation.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Haemodynamic instability mandates surgical management — MTX has slow onset and won't address active bleeding.

context:
Methotrexate management of stable, unruptured ectopic requires careful follow-up. After single-dose IM methotrexate (50 mg/m²), measure bhCG on day 4 and day 7. Day 4 bhCG often rises before falling — acceptable.

A day 4 to day 7 fall of 15% or more indicates response — continue weekly bhCG to undetectable. A fall of less than 15%: give a second methotrexate dose. Continued symptoms or rising bhCG: consider surgery.
